**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Patient presents with a 2-hour history of crushing, heavy central chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw, associated with profuse sweating and nausea. Patient drove themselves to the practice alone and is currently unaccompanied. Emergency escalation has been triggered.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) — classic presentation: crushing chest pain, left arm and jaw radiation, diaphoresis, nausea, 2-hour duration
2. Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) — same clinical picture, differentiated by ECG and troponin
3. Unstable angina — similar presentation but less likely given severity, duration, and associated autonomic features

*Also consider:*
• Aortic dissection — crushing chest/jaw pain can overlap; back pain not reported but not excluded
• Acute pericarditis — can present with chest pain, though radiation pattern and diaphoresis less typical

*Do not miss:*
⚠ STEMI with imminent haemodynamic compromise — patient is alone, drove themselves, has been symptomatic for 2 hours; time-critical
⚠ Aortic dissection — if ECG/troponin are not consistent with ACS, this must be actively excluded given the severity of presentation

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Immediate 12-lead ECG — look for ST elevation, new LBBB, or reciprocal changes
• Blood pressure both arms (discrepancy may suggest dissection)
• Pulse oximetry and heart rate
• Auscultate for new murmurs or pericardial rub
• Assess for signs of cardiogenic shock: pallor, cold peripheries, altered consciousness

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• 12-lead ECG — immediate, before anything else
• High-sensitivity troponin I or T — baseline and repeat at 1–3 hours
• FBC, U&E, glucose, lipid profile
• Chest X-ray — widened mediastinum would raise suspicion for dissection

*If first line inconclusive:*
• Repeat troponin at 3 and 6 hours
• CT pulmonary angiogram / CT aortogram if dissection not excluded

**Management Principles**
• Call EMS immediately if not already done — do not allow patient to drive
• Aspirin 300mg PO stat if no contraindication (do not delay for allergy history in this emergency)
• IV access, oxygen if SpO2 < 94%
• Urgent transfer to nearest facility with PCI capability — 2-hour symptom onset is still within reperfusion window
• GTN spray if systolic BP > 90mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor use

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
If ECG is non-diagnostic but symptoms persist, do not discharge — serial troponins and monitoring are mandatory. If pain changes character or BP discrepancy is found, escalate immediately to CT aorta to exclude Type A dissection.

Stay with your neighbour, keep the lights low, and don't open the door until the ambulance arrives. You're doing the right thing.

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Female patient presenting with a sudden-onset "thunderclap" headache of maximum severity, beginning approximately 3 hours ago — described as the worst headache of her life. Associated photophobia noted (unable to tolerate normal indoor lighting). No visual loss reported. Patient is alone at home; ambulance has been called and neighbour is present.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH)** — classic thunderclap onset, "worst headache of life," photophobia; this is SAH until proven otherwise
2. **Meningitis / meningoencephalitis** — photophobia fits; thunderclap onset less typical but cannot be excluded
3. **Hypertensive emergency with intracranial hypertension** — sudden severe headache with photophobia; BP unknown

*Also consider:*
• **Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)** — can present with sudden severe headache; important in women of childbearing age
• **Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCAS)** — recurrent thunderclap headaches; first episode indistinguishable from SAH

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Subarachnoid haemorrhage** — this presentation is SAH until CT and LP prove otherwise; a normal CT does not exclude SAH if done within 6 hours — LP for xanthochromia is required if CT is negative
⚠ **Neck stiffness / meningism** — not yet assessed; ER team must check for Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full neurological examination including GCS, cranial nerves, and focal deficits
• Meningism assessment: neck stiffness, Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's sign
• Fundoscopy: look for papilloedema or subhyaloid haemorrhage (strongly suggestive of SAH)
• Blood pressure (both arms)
• Temperature

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Non-contrast CT head — urgent; look for subarachnoid blood in basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures, or cortical sulci
• If CT negative and clinical suspicion remains high: LP at 12 hours from onset for xanthochromia and red cell count

*If first line inconclusive:*
• CT angiography or MR angiography — to identify aneurysm or vascular malformation
• MRI brain with FLAIR sequences if CVST suspected

**Management Principles**
• Immediate ER assessment and neurosurgical referral if SAH confirmed
• Strict bed rest, analgesia (avoid NSAIDs if SAH suspected — antiplatelet effect)
• Nimodipine if SAH confirmed (vasospasm prevention)
• Do not delay imaging for any reason

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
If CT is reported as normal, do not discharge without LP at ≥12 hours from headache onset — up to 3% of SAH cases are CT-negative in the first 6 hours. A missed SAH carries extremely high mortality on re-bleed.

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Third-party caller (husband) reporting on behalf of his wife. Patient collapsed approximately one hour ago and presented with two confirmed stroke symptoms: slurred speech and left-sided facial drooping. Onset was sudden, approximately one hour ago. Patient is currently conscious and awake. Husband is present with patient and has been directed to call emergency services immediately.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. Ischaemic stroke — sudden onset facial droop + slurred speech (dysarthria) with collapse; classic anterior circulation presentation
2. Haemorrhagic stroke (intracerebral haemorrhage) — clinically indistinguishable from ischaemic stroke at this stage; must be excluded urgently via CT
3. TIA (transient ischaemic attack) — if symptoms begin to resolve before hospital arrival; still requires emergency assessment and does not change immediate management

*Also consider:*
• Todd's paresis post-seizure — focal neurological deficit following a seizure; collapse history is consistent; enquire at hospital whether any witnessed convulsive activity occurred
• Hypoglycaemia — can mimic stroke with focal deficits and collapse; rapid BGL check in ER essential before thrombolysis decision

*Do not miss:*
⚠ Haemorrhagic stroke — thrombolysis is contraindicated; CT head before any treatment is mandatory
⚠ Basilar artery occlusion — can present atypically with collapse and dysarthria; carries very high mortality if missed; posterior circulation strokes may not score high on standard FAST screen

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full NIHSS (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale) assessment on arrival
• BP both arms — significant asymmetry may suggest aortic dissection with cerebral involvement
• BGL immediately on arrival
• Cranial nerve examination — specifically VII (facial), XII (tongue), and assess for gaze deviation
• Limb power and sensation — assess for hemiplegia not yet reported by caller
• Assess level of consciousness — GCS on arrival

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Non-contrast CT head — urgent, to exclude haemorrhage before any thrombolysis consideration
• BGL — immediate bedside test
• ECG — to identify atrial fibrillation as cardioembolic source
• FBC, coagulation screen, U&E, LFTs

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• CT angiography — to identify large vessel occlusion amenable to mechanical thrombectomy
• MRI brain with DWI — more sensitive for early ischaemic change, particularly posterior fossa
• Echocardiogram — to assess for cardiac embolic source (valvular disease, intracardiac thrombus)

**Management Principles**
• Time-critical: confirm last known well time (one hour ago per husband) — patient may be within thrombolysis window (≤4.5 hours) if haemorrhage excluded
• Activate stroke pathway on ER arrival
• Thrombolysis (IV alteplase) if ischaemic confirmed, no contraindications, and within window
• Consider mechanical thrombectomy referral if large vessel occlusion identified
• Monitor and maintain airway, BP, oxygen saturation, and glucose

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
Patient has been directed to emergency services and will not be presenting to the practice today. If patient or husband contacts the practice again before reaching hospital, re-emphasise calling 999/911 immediately and do not allow self-transport. If symptoms have fully resolved on arrival (possible TIA), patient still requires same-day emergency neurovascular assessment — do not discharge without TIA clinic or stroke unit review.

**Key History**
Patient presents with approximately 2 weeks of profound fatigue, low mood, hopelessness, anhedonia (including loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities), poor appetite, and psychomotor slowing with social withdrawal. **Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. Major Depressive Episode with suicidal ideation and specific plan — classic symptom cluster: anhedonia, hopelessness, anergia, poor appetite, unrefreshing sleep, social withdrawal, duration >2 weeks. Active plan significantly elevates risk.
2. Adjustment Disorder with depressed mood — if an identifiable stressor can be identified; however, the depth of symptoms and suicidal planning favour MDD over adjustment disorder.
3. Dysthymia (Persistent Depressive Disorder) with acute exacerbation — if background low mood predates this episode; worth exploring in appointment.

*Also consider:*
• Hypothyroidism — fatigue, low mood, poor appetite, and withdrawal can all be thyroid-mediated; TSH essential to exclude organic cause.
• Anaemia — especially relevant in SA context; fatigue and low mood may have a haematological contribution.
• HIV-related depression or HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder — HIV status not yet obtained; important to establish given SA prevalence.
• Substance use — alcohol or other substances can both cause and mask depressive symptoms; worth exploring sensitively in the appointment.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Active suicide risk with specific plan and means available** — patient has identified pills at home as method. This is HIGH risk. Means restriction counselling is urgent — advise patient or a trusted person to remove or secure the pills TODAY before they leave the practice. Consider whether voluntary or involuntary psychiatric admission is warranted.
⚠ **Bipolar Disorder (depressive phase)** — prescribing an antidepressant without ruling out bipolar history could precipitate a manic episode; ask specifically about any prior periods of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, or impulsive behaviour.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full mental state examination — appearance, affect, thought content, insight, judgement
• Assess suicide risk formally (e.g. Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale or equivalent)
• Thyroid palpation
• Vital signs including BMI/weight (nutritional impact of poor appetite)
• General appearance for signs of self-neglect or concealed self-harm

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• TSH — exclude hypothyroidism as organic contributor
• FBC — exclude anaemia
• Fasting glucose — exclude diabetes-related fatigue and low mood
• HIV test (if status unknown) — essential in SA context
• LFTs and U&E — baseline before considering pharmacotherapy

*If first line inconclusive:*
• Vitamin B12 and folate
• Ferritin
• Cortisol if adrenal insufficiency suspected

**Management Principles**
• **Immediate priority: means restriction** — address the pills at home today. Ask who is with the patient and whether a trusted person can secure or remove them urgently.
• Assess need for same-day psychiatric referral or admission given specific plan and available means.
• If outpatient management is deemed safe: initiate antidepressant (SSRI first line — consider escitalopram or sertraline), with close follow-up within 1 week.
• Safety planning: provide crisis line numbers (SADAG: 0800 456 789 / 0800 21 22 23), identify a support person.
• Explore social history, stressors, and prior psychiatric history in full during appointment.
• Rule out bipolar disorder before prescribing antidepressant alone.

**Safety Net for Dr. Patel**
If patient discloses escalating ideation, active intent, or inability to commit to a safety plan, consider urgent psychiatric referral or admission under the Mental Health Care Act (No. 17 of 2002). Do not allow patient to leave without a clear safety plan

Adult patient presenting with a 6-week productive cough with yellow-green sputum and haemoptysis (blood noted twice this week). Associated symptoms include drenching night sweats occurring nightly, and significant unintentional weight loss of approximately 5kg over the past month. The patient shares a room with a sibling who was treated for TB last year. No fever reported, no dyspnoea. Non-smoker, occasional alcohol use, no regular medications.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Pulmonary Tuberculosis** — 6-week productive cough, haemoptysis, drenching night sweats, significant weight loss, and direct close contact with a confirmed TB case (room-sharing with a sibling treated for TB last year). This clinical picture is highly consistent with active TB until proven otherwise.
2. **Bacterial pneumonia / persistent lower respiratory tract infection** — purulent (yellow-green) sputum of 6 weeks duration; however, the constellation of constitutional symptoms and TB contact makes simple bacterial infection less likely as the sole diagnosis.
3. **Post-primary TB reactivation** — particularly relevant if HIV-positive (status declined); reactivation TB can present with this exact picture.

*Also consider:*
• **Lung abscess** — persistent purulent sputum, haemoptysis, and prolonged course could indicate cavitating infection; may co-exist with or mimic TB.
• **Bronchiectasis** — chronic productive cough with purulent sputum; less likely to explain the weight loss and night sweats acutely.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **HIV-associated pulmonary disease** — patient declined HIV status discussion. Given the TB contact, constitutional symptoms, and haemoptysis, HIV co-infection significantly elevates TB risk and must be sensitively revisited by Dr. Patel. HIV status is critical for management decisions.
⚠ **Lung malignancy** — haemoptysis, weight loss, and a prolonged cough must always prompt consideration of malignancy, even in a younger patient. If sputum AFB and initial workup are negative, chest CT and further investigation are warranted.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full respiratory examination — percussion, auscultation for crackles, bronchial breathing, or reduced air entry (particularly in upper lobes, classic for TB)
• Check for lymphadenopathy — cervical, axillary, supraclavicular
• Assess BMI / current weight and document
• Temperature and full vital signs
• Examine for oral thrush or other signs of immunosuppression
• Inspect sputum if available

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• **Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF x2** — high sensitivity for TB; also detects rifampicin resistance. Priority investigation given clinical picture and TB contact.
• **Sputum microscopy and culture (AFB x3)** — standard TB workup
• **Chest X-ray** — look for upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, hilar lymphadenopathy, or consolidation
• **FBC, CRP, ESR** — to assess systemic inflammation and anaemia
• **HIV rapid test** — Dr. Patel to sensitively re-approach consent; essential for complete management

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• **CT chest** — if CXR non-diagnostic or to assess for malignancy/cavitation/lymphadenopathy
• **Bronchoscopy + BAL** — if sputum smear-negative but TB or malignancy still suspected

**Management Principles**
• If TB confirmed: initiate standard DOTS (2RHZE/4RH) as per SA National TB Guidelines; notify as per legal requirement
• Do not start TB treatment empirically without at least GeneXpert result if patient is stable enough to wait
• Address TB contact tracing — the brother who was treated last year may warrant reassessment for treatment completion and possible re-infection of the household
• HIV testing is strongly recommended — counsel patient on the importance in the context of TB
• Nutritional support — 5kg unintentional weight loss warrants nutritional assessment
• Safety net: if haemoptysis worsens significantly (large volume), advise urgent emergency

*Most likely:*

2. **Tension-type headache** — bilateral, dull, non-pulsating, not aggravated by routine activity, no nausea/photophobia; consistent with ICHD-3 criteria; stress and sleep deprivation are clear precipitants
3. **Alcohol-related fatigue and sleep disruption** — ~35 standard drinks/week (hazardous use); alcohol is a known disruptor of sleep architecture (reduces REM, causes early waking), and causes next-day fatigue; may be the primary driver being attributed to "stress"

- **Hypertension** — strong family history (father: MI at 58), daily smoking (20 pack-year history), hazardous alcohol use, sedentary lifestyle; headaches may have a hypertensive component; no BP recorded yet

*Most likely:*

• **Eclampsia (imminent)** — worsening headache + visual symptoms = high risk of seizure; escalation already initiated
• **Placental abruption** — reduced fetal movements could indicate placental compromise; must be excluded urgently

78-year-old female (assumed) with known cardiac disease presenting with acutely worsening exertional dyspnoea this week, now severely limiting her functional capacity (unable to walk to the kitchen without stopping). **Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)** — purulent, malodorous discharge + unilateral lower abdominal pain (left-sided) + no alternative explanation strongly suggests ascending genital tract infection; condom use reduces but does not eliminate STI risk.
2. **Bacterial Vaginosis (BV)** — malodorous, increased discharge is classic; however, BV alone does not typically cause lower abdominal pain, making this less likely as the sole diagnosis.
3. **Cervicitis (Chlamydia or Gonorrhoea)** — mucopurulent cervical discharge is consistent with both organisms; either can ascend to cause PID if untreated.

• **Trichomonas vaginalis** — can cause malodorous yellowish discharge, though typically associated with itching (absent here); worth excluding.

⚠ **Ectopic pregnancy** — left-sided pelvic pain in a woman of reproductive age must prompt exclusion; urine βhCG is mandatory even with consistent condom use and a normal LMP. Do not omit this.
⚠ **Tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA)** — a complication of untreated PID; if adnexal tenderness or mass is found on examination, urgent referral and imaging are required. Missing this can result in serious morbidity.

• Vital signs including temperature (fever supports PID/TOA)
• Abdominal examination: guarding, rebound tenderness, localised left iliac fossa tenderness
• Speculum examination: assess discharge colour, volume, cervical appearance (cervicitis, strawberry cervix for Trichomonas)
• Bimanual examination: cervical excitation tenderness (highly specific for PID), uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness or mass (left side especially)

• Urine βhCG — mandatory to exclude ectopic pregnancy before any other workup

**Key History**
Adult male (age not obtained — doctor to confirm), software developer, presenting after a first-ever witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure this morning while waking from sleep. Wife witnessed the event: tonic phase followed by clonic phase, approximately 2 minutes in duration. Patient had no prodrome and no recall of the event. Post-ictal confusion and headache noted (now resolving). Precipitating factors include significant sleep deprivation the night prior (approximately 3 hours). No prior seizure history, no regular medications, no family history of epilepsy. HIV negative (last tested ~2 years ago). Socially well, moderate alcohol intake (weekends only), non-smoker, physically active.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **First unprovoked generalised seizure (possible new-onset epilepsy)** — tonic-clonic semiology, no clear provoking cause beyond sleep deprivation, no structural symptoms reported, warrants full workup
2. **Provoked seizure secondary to sleep deprivation** — significant sleep deprivation is a well-recognised seizure threshold-lowering factor; if no structural or metabolic cause found, this becomes the most likely precipitant
3. **Metabolic/electrolyte disturbance** — hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, or other metabolic derangement can precipitate first seizures; no dietary history obtained to assess

*Also consider:*
• **Alcohol-related seizure** — social drinking reported, but patient denies heavy or recent cessation use; worth clarifying exact pattern and whether last drink was unusually recent or pattern has changed
• **Structural brain lesion (tumour, AVM, cortical dysplasia)** — wake-from-sleep seizures can be associated with focal cortical pathology; absence of focal neurology is reassuring but does not exclude

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Intracranial pathology (tumour, subdural haematoma, vascular malformation)** — first seizure in an adult always requires neuroimaging to exclude structural cause regardless of apparent good health
⚠ **Encephalitis or CNS infection** — no fever or meningism reported, but post-ictal headache and a first seizure warrant consideration; LP if neuroimaging normal and any concern remains

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Full neurological examination — cranial nerves, tone, power, reflexes, plantar responses, coordination; look for any focal deficit suggesting structural lesion
• Assess level of consciousness and orientation fully — confirm complete post-ictal recovery
• Tongue/cheek laceration and shoulder tenderness — assess for injury sustained during seizure
• Blood pressure both arms — hypertensive encephalopathy is rare but worth excluding
• Temperature and meningeal signs — Kernig's and Brudzinski's, even in absence of reported neck stiffness

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• **Blood glucose** — exclude hypoglycaemia as precipitant
• **FBC, U&E, LFTs, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, phosphate** — metabolic screen for provoked seizure
• **ECG** — exclude cardiac arrhythmia mimicking seizure (though witnessed tonic-clonic makes this less likely)
• **Urgent MRI brain (or CT brain if MRI not immediately available)** — mandatory for first adult seizure to exclude structural pathology

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• **EEG** — ideally within 24–48 hours; sleep-deprived EEG increases yield
• **LP** — if any suspicion of encephalitis or CNS infection after neuroimaging

**Management Principles**
• Do not start anti-epileptic medication at this visit — single provoked seizure does not automatically warrant treatment; neurology input needed
• Refer urgently to neurology for first seizure workup
• Counsel patient clearly: **do not drive** until seizure-free for the legally required period (in South Africa, typically 6 months seizure-free and cleared by a doctor before driving is permitted) — this must be communicated explicitly today
• Advise avoiding known threshold-lowering triggers: sleep deprivation, excess alcohol, excessive screen/shift

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Adult patient (teacher by occupation) presenting with a 1-day history of right eye redness, mild-to-moderate soreness, and itchiness, with yellow mucopurulent discharge and morning crusting. No photophobia, no visual disturbance, no deep eye pain, and no recent URTI. Son had an identical presentation one week ago, strongly suggesting a contagious aetiology. No regular medications. Penicillin allergy (rash). HIV negative (tested ~1 year ago). Otherwise well, no chronic conditions.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Bacterial conjunctivitis** — unilateral onset, yellow mucopurulent discharge, morning crusting, household contact with same illness, no photophobia or visual loss. Classic presentation.
2. **Viral conjunctivitis** — can also present with redness and discharge; typically more watery, but mucopurulent discharge does not exclude viral (especially adenoviral). Household contact supports contagious viral spread.
3. **Allergic conjunctivitis** — itchiness is present, but discharge is yellow/mucopurulent rather than clear/watery, no known allergen exposure, no personal or family history of atopy. Less likely but worth considering.

*Also consider:*
- **Chlamydial conjunctivitis** — can cause chronic or subacute mucopurulent conjunctivitis; less likely given acute onset but worth considering if it fails to respond to standard topical treatment.
- **Mixed bacterial/viral** — co-infection possible, especially in community/school exposure context.

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Acute angle-closure glaucoma** — patient denies deep eye pain, nausea, haloes around lights, and has no visual disturbance; clinical picture does not support this, but worth a brief IOP/anterior chamber check if any atypical features on examination.
⚠ **Keratitis (corneal involvement)** — no photophobia or visual change reported, but slit-lamp or fluorescein staining should be considered if the eye does not improve with treatment, or if examination reveals corneal haziness, to exclude bacterial or viral (HSV) keratitis.

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
- Visual acuity both eyes (Snellen chart)
- Examination of conjunctiva: note injection pattern (limbal sparing vs. diffuse), presence and character of discharge, papillae vs. follicles on eversion of the upper lid (follicles suggest viral/chlamydial; papillae suggest bacterial or allergic)
- Corneal clarity — check for haziness or ulceration; consider fluorescein staining if any doubt
- Pre-auricular lymph node palpation — enlargement favours viral (adenoviral) aetiology
- Check pupil reactions and consensual reflex

**Investigations**
*First line:*
- Clinical diagnosis only is appropriate in straightforward bacterial conjunctivitis — no investigation needed if presentation is classic and responds to treatment.

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
- Conjunctival swab for MC&S — if no response to topical antibiotics within 48–72 hours, or if chlamydial infection suspected (add NAAT/PCR for *Chlamydia trachomatis*)
- Consider STI screen if chlamydial conjunctivitis is suspected

**Management Principles**
- If bacterial conjunctivitis confirmed clinically: topical antibiotic drops (e.g. chloramphenicol 0.5% drops QID for 5–7 days, or fusidic acid gel BD — bearing in mind penicillin allergy does not affect these choices)
- Advise strict hand hygiene and avoidance of sharing towels/pillowcases — highly contagious
- Advise patient that son should also be seen if not already treated
- Self-limiting if viral — supportive care (cold compresses, lubricating drops); antibiotics not indicated for pure viral conjunctivitis
- Safety net: return if vision changes, pain worsens, photophobia develops, or no improvement in 48 hours

conversation.content: My big toe is killing me. It's red and swollen and I can't put weight on it.

Oh no, that sounds really painful — I'm sorry to hear that.

Just before we go further — do you have any allergies to medicines or foods?
No, I don't have any allergies.

Good to know, thanks.

Can you tell me which foot it is — the left or the right?
It's the right one.

Got it.

How long has your right big toe been like this?
Since last night — woke up this morning and it was absolutely killing me.

Ouch, that sounds like it came on very suddenly overnight.

What does the pain feel like — is it sharp, dull, burning, or throbbing?
It's sharp and throbbing, mostly. Sharp when I try to move it or put any weight on it.

Right, got it.

On a scale of 1 to 10 — where 1 is barely there and 10 is the worst — how bad is the pain?
It's a 9, mate. Really bad. Can barely walk.

That sounds absolutely awful — a 9 is really severe.

Did anything happen to the toe before this started — like a knock, a knock, or an injury of any kind?
No, nothing like that. I just woke up with it like this. No injury or anything.

I see.

Have you ever had anything like this happen before — in this toe or anywhere else?
Yeah, actually — about a year ago I had the same thing. Same toe, same deal. Woke up in agony.

Okay, thanks for mentioning that.

When it happened last year, did a doctor give you any treatment or diagnosis for it?
Not really — I don't remember exactly what they said, to be honest. It just cleared up after a few days on its own, more or less.

Right, got it.

Has the toe changed at all since you woke up this morning — is it more swollen, or about the same?
About the same, I'd say. Still red and warm to touch, but it hasn't really gotten worse or better since I woke up.

I see, okay.

Have you noticed any fever — feeling hot, shivery, or generally unwell with it?
No fever, no. I feel alright otherwise — it's just the toe that's the problem.

Good to know, that's helpful.

Did you have anything different to eat or drink in the day or two before this started — like a big meal, shellfish, red meat, or more alcohol than usual?
Yeah, actually — I had a braai this weekend, lots of red meat. That's probably not helped, has it?

I'll make sure the doctor has all of that information.

Are you on any medicines at the moment — anything at all, whether prescription or something you buy yourself?
Yeah, I take allopurinol 300mg once a day. Been on that for about a year now.
Okay, thanks. And how long have you been taking the allopurinol — since around the time you had that first episode a year ago?
Yeah, around about that time, yeah. Started it a year ago or so.

Got it, thanks.

Are you taking any other medicines — anything else at all, even vitamins or supplements?
No, just the allopurinol. That's it.

Okay, good.

Do you smoke at all?
Yeah, I do — about 15 a day.
Okay. And how about alcohol — do you drink, and roughly how much in a typical week?
Yeah, I drink quite a bit — maybe 5 or 6 beers most days, so... yeah, quite a lot really.

Right, thanks for being honest about that — it's really helpful for the doctor to know.

Who do you live with at home — are you on your own or with family?
I live with my wife. It's just the two of us.

Okay, good.

Now, has anyone in your family had problems with gout, heart disease, diabetes, or high blood pressure?
My father had gout, yeah. So it runs in the family a bit.

That's really useful to know.

Has anyone in your family had heart disease, diabetes, or high blood pressure — any of those?
Not that I'm aware of, no. Just the gout with my dad.

Okay, thanks.

We ask all our patients about HIV at this clinic because it helps us give you the best care — there's no wrong answer. Do you know your HIV status?
No, I'm negative. I've never had any issues with that.

Thanks for letting me know.

Do you use any traditional medicines, herbs, or see a traditional healer? Some can interact with clinic medicines, so it's useful to know.
No, I don't use any of that stuff. Just what the doctor gives me.

Good to know.

Before I pass everything over to the doctor, I just have three quick general questions.

How has your sleep been lately — do you feel rested when you wake up?
Sleep's been fine, nothing wrong there. I'm just woken up by this toe pain, obviously.

Ha, yes, that's completely understandable!

How have you been feeling emotionally — any stress or tough times recently?
No, nothing major. Just the usual work stuff. Nothing out of the ordinary.

Glad to hear it's nothing too heavy.

Do you manage to get any exercise or physical activity during the week?
Not much, to be honest. I'm not really doing anything regular. Maybe a bit of walking around work, but that's about it.

Okay, thanks for that.

[HISTORY_COMPLETE]

---

**CLINICAL SUMMARY FOR DR. PATEL**

**Key History**
Male patient presenting with a sudden-onset acutely painful, red, swollen, and warm right first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, waking him from sleep overnight — rated 9/10 in severity. No preceding trauma. Identical episode in the same joint approximately one year ago, which resolved spontaneously. Precipitating factors include a large red meat-heavy braai and significant ongoing alcohol use (5–6 beers daily) over the weekend. Currently on allopurinol 300mg once daily (commenced ~1 year ago). Father has gout. HIV negative. Non-smoker... correction: smokes approximately 15 cigarettes per day. No fever or systemic upset.

**Differential Diagnosis**
*Most likely:*
1. **Acute gout flare** — classic podagra presentation; first MTP joint, nocturnal onset, extreme pain, warmth and erythema, prior identical episode, positive family history, high purine/alcohol intake as clear precipitant, already on allopurinol (flares can still occur on allopurinol, particularly in the first year of treatment or if dose is subtherapeutic)
2. **Subtherapeutic allopurinol / poor urate control** — flare occurring despite allopurinol suggests serum uric acid may not be at target (<0.36 mmol/L); dose may need uptitration or adherence may be an issue
3. **Septic arthritis** — must be considered in any hot, swollen, acutely painful joint; absence of fever and systemic upset lowers probability but does not exclude it

*Also consider:*
• **Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition)** — less typical in first MTP joint but possible; usually affects larger joints such as knee or wrist
• **Reactive arthritis** — unlikely given no preceding infection history, but worth noting if joint aspirate is negative for crystals

*Do not miss:*
⚠ **Septic arthritis** — even without fever, this must be excluded before assuming gout; a joint aspirate is the only way to definitively distinguish; if septic arthritis is missed, joint destruction can occur rapidly
⚠ **Cardiovascular risk profile** — this patient has significant, under-recognised cardiovascular risk: heavy daily alcohol use (35–42 units/week, well above safe limits), active smoking (15/day), sedentary lifestyle, gout (independent CV risk factor), and possible metabolic syndrome; this visit is an opportunity to address the broader risk profile

**Suggested Clinical Examination**
• Examine right first MTP joint: erythema, swelling, warmth, range of motion, tenderness — classic podagra appearance
• Check for tophi: ears, elbows, fingers, Achilles tendons
• Blood pressure — likely elevated given alcohol, smoking, and gout
• BMI and waist circumference — assess for metabolic syndrome
• Examine for any signs of systemic infection (lymphadenopathy, skin breaks near the joint)

**Investigations**
*First line:*
• Serum uric acid — to assess current control on allopurinol (target <0.36 mmol/L); note: may be falsely low during an acute flare
• FBC — to check for raised WCC suggesting infection or systemic inflammation
• CRP / ESR — inflammatory marker baseline
• Renal function (urea, creatinine, eGFR) — important given allopurinol use and high alcohol intake; gout is associated with renal impairment
• Fasting glucose and lipids — screen for metabolic syndrome given overall risk profile
• LFTs — given 35–42 units of alcohol per week

*If first line inconclusive or diagnosis remains unclear:*
• Joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis (Gram stain, culture, microscopy for urate crystals) — gold standard to distinguish gout from septic arthritis
• X-ray right foot — may show soft tissue swelling; chronic gouty changes (punched-out erosions) if longstanding

**Management Principles**
• Acute flare: NSAIDs (e.g. naproxen 500mg BD with food) if renal function adequate, or colchicine 500
